summaries.headline: What Sets Top Reading Schools Apart
summaries.summary: The 74's Bright Spots series set out a year ago to identify schools that beat demographic odds in teaching kids to read, and a review of those schools surfaced recurring traits tied to strong literacy outcomes. Common threads include stable, instructionally-focused leadership, an emphasis on foundational skills like phonics, and consistently high expectations for all students regardless of zip code or poverty rate. As debates swirl over whether a media-saturated, AI-driven world is making reading less essential, these schools offer a counterpoint grounded in practice rather than theory — proof that the fundamentals of reading instruction still travel well across different contexts.

summaries.headline: U.S. PISA Rank Climbs as Global Scores Sink
summaries.summary: U.S. students now score above average in reading and science on the latest PISA results, with math finally matching other developed countries after decades as the country's weakest subject. The gain isn't from American students learning more — U.S. math and reading scores sit at or near record lows, and the country moved up mainly because other nations' scores fell faster over the past decade. Researchers point to a global decline with a long pandemic tail, meaning whatever is eroding learning here likely isn't a uniquely American problem, and celebrating the ranking shift risks masking a shared crisis in student achievement.

summaries.headline: Districts Seek Literacy Screeners, STEM Evaluators
summaries.summary: Spokane Public Schools in Washington is soliciting a K-2 literacy universal screening tool to meet state dyslexia screening requirements, with proposals due Sept. 25 covering phonemic awareness, phonological awareness, and letter-sound knowledge assessment across the district's 28,700 students. Passaic City Public Schools in New Jersey, serving 12,790 students, is separately seeking an external evaluator for its STEM after-school program on the same deadline, while a Missouri district searches for a middle school health curriculum. The overlapping timelines show districts simultaneously prioritizing early literacy diagnostics and program accountability measures as they head into procurement season.

summaries.headline: AI Guidance Gap Leaves Teachers, Students Behind
summaries.summary: Microsoft's third annual AI in Education report finds nearly 9 in 10 students, educators and leaders have used AI for school, but daily use splits sharply by role: over half of leaders use it daily compared with about a third of teachers and a quarter of students. The bigger disconnect is on training and guidance—4 in 5 leaders say their institution's AI direction is clear, yet half of students and teachers call it nonexistent or neutral, and while 70% of leaders believe at least half their staff and students have received formal AI training, 77% of students and 53% of educators say they've gotten none. Leaders think they're communicating policy and building capacity; the people actually using the tools say otherwise, a mismatch that likely explains why adoption is broad but confidence remains shallow.

summaries.headline: NC Graduation Rate Hits Record 88.8%
summaries.summary: North Carolina's State Board of Education reviewed 2025-26 accountability data this week showing the statewide graduation rate climbed a full percentage point to 88.8%, the highest mark in state history. Board members also dug into chronic absenteeism trends, technology policies and grants, special education updates, and a budget briefing from Winston-Salem/Forsyth County Schools, signaling that attendance and tech infrastructure remain as central to the state's improvement agenda as test scores. The graduation milestone gives DPI leadership momentum toward its "Best in Nation" strategic goal, but the parallel focus on absenteeism suggests officials know attendance gaps could undercut those gains if left unaddressed.

summaries.headline: Denver Board Confronts Antisemitism Allegation, Deep Discord
summaries.summary: The Denver school board publicly grappled with allegations that Vice President Monica Hunter used antisemitic language toward a colleague, part of a broader list of policy violations President Xóchitl Gaytán raised against Hunter and board member DJ Torres, including missed meetings, disparaging social media posts, and bypassing the chain of command with district staff. Both accused members call the claims baseless and exaggerated, and while most board members said they take the allegations seriously, none committed to how they'd vote on a possible censure set for September 17, with Superintendent Alex Marrero — who raised his own concerns this summer about board overreach — offering to provide testimonials. The public airing of dysfunction, capped by member Amy Klein Molk's call for the board to "model how people can disagree without hatred," underscores how governance conflict at the top can overshadow the district's actual work.

summaries.headline: Denver Board Infighting Escalates to Formal Misconduct Charges
summaries.summary: Denver school board president Xóchitl Gaytán has formally accused Vice President Monica Hunter and board member DJ Torres of multiple policy violations, including allegations that Hunter used antisemitic language toward a colleague and improperly intervened in her own son's school transfer, while Torres allegedly missed meetings repeatedly. Board policy requires public discussion of the accusations before any censure vote, and both members have denied wrongdoing, with Hunter calling the charges "baseless" and warning that such claims risk being weaponized to discredit board members. The dispute, set for public airing at Wednesday's meeting, underscores deepening dysfunction on the board governing Colorado's largest school district at a moment when student outcomes should be commanding its full attention.

summaries.headline: New NYC Early Childhood Chief Inherits 2-K Crisis
summaries.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani named Erica Phillips, a nonprofit leader with experience supporting family childcare providers, as deputy chancellor for the Education Department's Division of Early Childhood Education just two days before the school year began. Phillips steps into a division still working through a severe contract payment backlog that pushed some providers to the brink of closure, even as the city's free 2-K program prepares to grow from 2,000 toddlers this year to a projected 12,000 by next fall. Her handling of the sprawling, disjointed childcare system will shape whether Mamdani's signature policy pledge — universal 2-K access by the end of his first term — survives its shaky launch and uncertain state funding beyond year two.

summaries.headline: NYC Classrooms Trade Novels for Test Prep
summaries.summary: New York City teachers say full-length novels have all but disappeared from English classes, replaced by excerpts, short passages, and standardized test-prep exercises that leave no room for sustained reading. One veteran middle school teacher described students spending half of each 40-minute period on an online reading intervention program — often disengaged, clicking through to Spotify or YouTube instead — while her once-active classroom library now sits "purely decorative," with books being discarded. District officials point to a 14 percent rise in digital book checkouts as evidence students still access full texts, but the shift toward curricula like HMH Into Reading, which doesn't require novel studies, raises questions about whether test-focused programming is quietly eroding the reading stamina and engagement schools say they want to build.

summaries.headline: NYC Schools Roll Out AI, Screen Time Limits
summaries.summary: New York City schools opened this week under a new policy banning generative AI tools like chatbots in preschool through eighth grade, with limited AI use allowed only in high school. Individual devices are prohibited through second grade, capped at 30 minutes daily in grades 3-5, and 45 minutes in middle school, though high schools face no screen time guidelines at all. Parents interviewed by Chalkbeat welcomed the rules as backup for battles they already fight at home, even as city officials have offered few details on how compliance will be tracked or enforced across more than 1,600 schools.

summaries.headline: Five Groups Unite on Ed Tech Vetting Standards
summaries.summary: Digital Promise, 1EdTech, CAST, CoSN, ISTE and SETDA have jointly released an EdTech Quality Indicators Guide to help district leaders cut through the crowded ed tech market with evidence-based procurement decisions. The framework scores tools against five criteria: safety and data privacy, research-backed evidence, inclusivity and accessible design, intuitive usability, and interoperability with existing systems through open data standards. For IT leaders juggling limited budgets and mounting vendor pitches, a shared, field-vetted checklist offers a common language for procurement teams and school boards to justify — or reject — a purchase before it's locked into a multiyear contract.

summaries.headline: Educators to Advise Pennsylvania on Literacy, Funding
summaries.summary: Nearly 50 Pre-K-12 educators across Pennsylvania, including three from the Lehigh Valley, will spend the next year working directly with state policymakers on issues like literacy and school funding through Teach Plus Pennsylvania's 2026-27 Policy Fellowship. The local cohort includes Denisha Bolden from Bethlehem Area School District and Jenna Miller and Lynn Unger from Lehigh Valley Children's Centers, alongside fellows from the Poconos region. The initiative signals a broader push to ground state education policy in classroom-level experience rather than top-down mandates alone.

summaries.headline: Opinion: Texas Must Fund Schools Before Vouchers
summaries.summary: An opinion piece in the Austin American-Statesman argues Texas lawmakers should address chronic public school funding shortfalls before expanding the state's new private school voucher program. The piece comes as Texas school districts continue to report budget gaps tied to stagnant per-pupil funding formulas that haven't kept pace with inflation, even as the state moves forward with education savings accounts that will direct public dollars to private education. The debate underscores a tension playing out in statehouses nationwide: whether school choice expansion and public school investment can be pursued simultaneously or whether one comes at the other's expense.

summaries.headline: California's Literacy Training List Draws Fire
summaries.summary: California's State Board of Education is set to approve a list of 37 professional development programs to train TK-5 teachers in science-of-reading instruction, a central piece of the state's multiyear literacy overhaul. Critics say the list is too broad and includes programs with low evidence ratings, effectively shifting the burden of vetting quality providers onto individual districts rather than the state. With districts already stretched thin, the gap between a state-sanctioned list and a truly vetted one could determine how consistently the science of reading actually reaches classrooms.

summaries.headline: California Approves 31 Literacy Training Providers
summaries.summary: The California State Board of Education approved 31 training programs districts can use to teach elementary teachers the science of reading, tapping into $200 million Gov. Gavin Newsom set aside last year for this purpose. Literacy reform advocates had pushed for a shorter, more selective list, arguing that quality control matters more than options when it comes to retraining teachers in phonics-based instruction. With districts now free to choose from a broad menu of approved providers, the consistency and rigor of implementation will likely vary widely from one classroom to the next.

summaries.headline: Extreme Heat Cuts Into Kids' Study Time
summaries.summary: A new study from IIT Guwahati's Prof. Bhaskar Jyoti Neog finds that extreme temperatures shift children's daily time allocation away from learning and toward leisure. Drawing on India's nationally representative Time Use Survey, the research identifies temperature extremes as a distinct and underexamined pathway through which climate change affects children's human capital formation, alongside its more visible impacts on attendance. As heat waves grow more frequent and severe across India, the findings point to instructional time itself as a climate casualty, not just school infrastructure or calendars.

summaries.headline: Colorado's Largest Homeschool Enrichment Program Shuts Down
summaries.summary: Colorado Homeschool Enrichment, which enrolled nearly 2,800 students across 48 campuses last year, will not operate this season after its authorizer dissolved and state officials imposed a stricter approval process for such programs. The program had drawn roughly $15 million in state funding annually, but scrutiny intensified after some campuses used public dollars for activities like skiing and horseback riding, and even funneled money to private school students. CHE's collapse lands as state officials draft new rules that could require publicly funded homeschool enrichment programs to operate under public entities like districts or charter schools, a shift that would reshape—or eliminate—the private operator model CHE represented.

summaries.headline: Mendham Schools Partner on Mental Health Strategy
summaries.summary: Mendham Borough School District has joined a three-year initiative with The Jed Foundation and AASA, the School Superintendents Association, to assess and strengthen student mental health supports. The program starts with a comprehensive evaluation of the district's existing programs and practices, drawing on input from district leadership before officials build a customized strategic plan. Superintendent Mitzi Morillo framed the move as treating emotional well-being as inseparable from academic capacity, a signal that districts are increasingly formalizing mental health work rather than treating it as an ancillary support service.

summaries.headline: California Student Data Privacy Bill Awaits Newsom's Signature
summaries.summary: California lawmakers have passed AB 1159, the Learner Personal Information Protection Act, sending it to Governor Newsom's desk with a September 30 signing deadline. The bill extends privacy protections across the full pre-K-through-college pipeline, restricting how educational institutions and companies can collect, use, and share student data amid growing concerns about generative AI and ed-tech platforms harvesting sensitive information—data that in some cases has reportedly been sold to third parties for predatory marketing, including high-cost loans. For district leaders already navigating a patchwork of vendor contracts and AI tools in classrooms, the bill signals that California intends to tighten the rules on commercial data exploitation well before federal guidance catches up.
